title: The X-ray catalogue of FGK stars within 10 pc: The coronal temperature-brightness relation explained with the RTV scaling law
summary: A comprehensive measurement of stellar X-ray emission has important implications for our understanding of stellar dynamos, exoplanet atmosphere loss, and evaporation of protoplanetary disks. We present a catalogue of X-ray detections of the FGK-type main-sequence stars within 10 pc, which accounts for stellar multiplicity and optical loading of the detectors. To build the X-ray catalogue, we analysed all observations from SRG (Spectrum Roentgen Gamma)/eROSITA and XMM-Newton for stars in the FGK 10pc sample, and we cross-matched the sample with ROSAT catalogues. We fit thermal plasma models to the X-ray spectra to derive X-ray fluxes and coronal temperatures. We investigate the relation between coronal temperature and X-ray surface flux and find the result to be consistent with the ranges covered by different types of solar coronal magnetic structures. The lower end of the temperature-brightness relation is defined by the Maunder minimum star HD 166620 and three other stars whose positions identify them as possible Maunder minimum candidates. We identify systematic differences between the temperature-brightness law derived from XMM-Newton and eROSITA data that we attribute to their different instrumental response functions. We study the impact of both short-term flaring and long-term activity cycles on the evolution of coronal temperature along with X-ray brightness. With the exception of three stars, a remarkably small scatter is observed in the temperature-brightness relation across the whole sample. A natural explanation of the empirical kT-FX relation is provided by the RTV scaling law defined for solar magnetic loops. The small spread of the observed relation indicates a universal scaling between the length and the filling factor of coronal loops. The three observed outliers deviate from this invariance of the ratio of loop length to filling factor for an as of yet unknown reason.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive X-ray catalogue of FGK-type main-sequence stars within 10 pc, using data from eROSITA, XMM-Newton, and ROSAT. The authors fit thermal plasma models to derive X-ray fluxes and coronal temperatures, and investigate the coronal temperature–X-ray surface flux relation, finding it consistent with solar coronal magnetic structure ranges and explainable by the RTV scaling law for solar magnetic loops. They identify systematic differences between XMM-Newton and eROSITA responses, study flaring and activity cycle effects, and note three outliers deviating from the universal loop length-to-filling-factor invariance.
AI.motivation: A comprehensive measurement of stellar X-ray emission is important for understanding stellar dynamos, exoplanet atmosphere loss, and protoplanetary disk evaporation. A complete, multiplicities-accounted X-ray catalogue of nearby FGK main-sequence stars enables robust studies of coronal physics and activity across stellar samples.
AI.method: All eROSITA and XMM-Newton observations for the FGK 10 pc sample were analyzed, cross-matched with ROSAT catalogues, and stellar multiplicity and optical loading were accounted for. Thermal plasma models were fit to X-ray spectra to derive X-ray fluxes and coronal temperatures, and the temperature-brightness relation was examined.
AI.result: The temperature–X-ray surface flux relation is consistent with ranges of different solar coronal magnetic structures. The lower boundary is set by Maunder minimum star HD 166620 and three candidate Maunder minimum stars. Systematic temperature-brightness differences exist between XMM-Newton and eROSITA due to instrumental response differences. Except for three outliers, the sample exhibits remarkably small scatter in the temperature-brightness relation, explained by the RTV scaling law implying a universal loop length-to-filling-factor ratio.
AI.conclusion: The observed kT-FX relation is naturally explained by the RTV scaling law for solar magnetic loops, indicating a universal scaling between coronal loop length and filling factor. Three outliers deviate from this invariance for an as-yet-unknown reason, warranting further investigation.

title: Superdiffusion at the Galactic Centre
summary: Tracking S-star cluster orbits around Sgr A* calibrates orbital transport models for space-borne gravitational wave detectors. Standard kinetic theories model this cluster via local Fokker-Planck equations, which predict that general relativistic precession halts angular momentum diffusion at the Schwarzschild barrier. Because inverse-square gravitational encounters generate a Holtsmark torque distribution with infinite variance, resonant relaxation operates as a space-fractional process governed by non-local Lévy flights. We simulate this superdiffusive continuous-time random walk using a Markov chain initialized with empirical S-star orbits, including the recently observd S301. Integro-differential fractional operators allow trajectories to cross regions of quenched local diffusion without density buildup at the barrier. Non-equilibrium regimes yield immediate linear flux growth, while secular tidal heating at periastron inflates stellar radii to shift disruption boundaries. Regularized backward integration of the fractional transport equation traces current phase space configurations back to initial deposition states, matching the energy requirements of the \emph{Fermi} bubbles. Relativistic precession does not suppress mass-ratio inspiral rates, which provides a model for event topologies in target galactic nuclei.

AI.tldr: This paper models the S-star cluster around Sgr A* using a space-fractional (Lévy flight) transport framework rather than standard local Fokker-Planck kinetics. Because inverse-square encounters produce a Holtsmark torque distribution with infinite variance, resonant relaxation is non-local and superdiffusive, allowing orbits to cross the Schwarzschild barrier. Markov-chain simulations seeded with empirical S-star orbits (including S301) reproduce linear flux growth, periastron tidal radius inflation, Fermi bubble energetics via backward integration, and mass-ratio inspiral rates relevant to future gravitational wave detectors.
AI.motivation: Standard local Fokker-Planck theories predict that general relativistic precession halts angular momentum diffusion at the Schwarzschild barrier, yet observed S-star cluster behavior demands a transport model that accounts for non-local, superdiffusive dynamics. Tracking S-star orbits also calibrates orbital transport models for space-borne gravitational wave detectors.
AI.method: The authors treat resonant relaxation as a space-fractional continuous-time random walk governed by non-local Lévy flights, simulated via a Markov chain initialized with empirical S-star orbits including the recently observed S301. They employ integro-differential fractional operators to allow trajectories to cross quenched local diffusion regions, and use regularized backward integration of the fractional transport equation to map current phase-space configurations to initial deposition states.
AI.result: The model yields immediate linear flux growth in non-equilibrium regimes, inflates stellar radii via secular tidal heating at periastron (shifting disruption boundaries), matches Fermi bubble energy requirements through backward-traced initial states, and shows that relativistic precession does not suppress mass-ratio inspiral rates.
AI.conclusion: Fractional (non-local) transport accurately captures S-star cluster dynamics that local Fokker-Planck theory cannot, including barrier crossing, and provides a framework for modeling event topologies in target galactic nuclei relevant to gravitational wave detection.

title: JWST's Constraints on the Substellar IMF in NGC 2024
summary: A recent study has reported the detection of a turnover in the initial mass function (IMF) below 12 Mjup and the possible detection of a minimum mass near 3 Mjup in the heavily embedded cluster NGC 2024 (<1 Myr), which was based on a sample of brown dwarf candidates in NIRCam images from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). I have used those NIRCam data in conjunction with archival spectra from JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) to constrain the substellar IMF in NGC 2024. I present NIRSpec data for 87 sources, 67 of which are within the NIRCam field. Based on those spectra and data from previous studies (e.g., X-ray emission), I have classified 45 of the NIRSpec targets as members of NGC 2024, 17 of which have spectral types indicative of brown dwarfs (M6.5-L; 13 are within NIRCam). The latter have mass estimates as low as 4 Mjup according to theoretical evolutionary models. There remain a few photometric candidates lacking spectra that extend down to the completeness limit of the images (>=2 Mjup for Ak>=1), so the minimum mass of the IMF has not been detected. It is not possible to measure a reliable substellar IMF from the NIRCam images because of the small number of brown dwarfs encompassed by them, a bias against objects at lower masses due to the high extinctions, and incompleteness at >=10 Mjup due to the saturation limit. Thus, there is no evidence in the JWST data for a turnover below 12jup.

AI.tldr: This paper re-examines claims of an IMF turnover below 12 Mjup and a possible minimum mass near 3 Mjup in NGC 2024 using JWST NIRSpec spectra. The author classified 45 sources as cluster members (17 brown dwarfs with masses as low as 4 Mjup), but found insufficient evidence for a substellar IMF turnover due to small sample sizes, extinction bias, saturation incompleteness, and unobserved photometric candidates down to the completeness limit. The minimum mass of the IMF and the claimed turnover are not detected.
AI.motivation: To test the recent claim of an IMF turnover below 12 Mjup and a possible minimum mass near 3 Mjup in the young embedded cluster NGC 2024, which was based solely on NIRCam photometric candidates, by adding spectroscopic confirmation from NIRSpec.
AI.method: Using JWST NIRSpec archival spectra for 87 sources (67 within the NIRCam field) combined with NIRCam photometry and previous X-ray data to spectroscopically confirm membership and derive spectral types and mass estimates via theoretical evolutionary models.
AI.result: 45 sources classified as members, 17 of which are brown dwarfs (M6.5-L) with masses down to ~4 Mjup. Several photometric candidates remain unspectroscopically confirmed down to the completeness limit (~2 Mjup). Reliable substellar IMF measurement is impossible due to small numbers, extinction bias against low-mass objects, and saturation incompleteness at >=10 Mjup. No turnover below 12 Mjup is supported.
AI.conclusion: The JWST data do not provide evidence for an IMF turnover below 12 Mjup or a detected minimum IMF mass in NGC 2024; the earlier photometric claims are not substantiated by spectroscopic analysis.

title: X-ray Absorption Variability in NGC 1142: Another Constraint on the Nature of the Torus/Broad-Line Region in Active Galactic Nuclei
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: The physics, geometry, and kinematics of the gas and dust surrounding the central engine of active galactic nuclei (AGN) are not well understood. In some sources, this material obscures the coronal X-ray emission, allowing its line-of-sight column density ($N_H$) to be measured. Many sources display $N_H$ variability across multiple epochs. Studying this variability can provide information about the distribution and dynamics of the obscuring material. Particularly, previous works have shown that the probability of observing $N_H$ variability increases with the number of observations available. Additionally, the observed magnitudes of the $N_H$ variability depend on the timescale between observations. In this work, we present the $N_H$ variability analysis of NGC 1142, which has a total of nine X-ray observations over $\sim20$ years, including five from a NuSTAR+XMM-Newton monitoring campaign performed in 2024-2025 and reported here for the first time. We use the physically-motivated torus models UXCLUMPY, XSKIRTor, and RXTorusD to model the spectra. Our results confirm the previously observed trends, and we compare these trends to simulated obscuration curves assuming different locations and distributions of obscuring clouds.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the X-ray column density (NH) variability analysis of the AGN NGC 1142 using nine observations spanning ~20 years, including five new NuSTAR+XMM-Newton monitoring observations from 2024-2025. The authors model the spectra with physically-motivated torus models (UXCLUMPY, XSKIRTor, RXTorusD) and confirm previously observed trends, comparing them to simulated obscuration curves for different cloud distributions.
AI.motivation: To better understand the physics, geometry, and kinematics of gas and dust surrounding AGN central engines by studying NH variability, which provides information about the distribution and dynamics of the obscuring material.
AI.method: The authors analyze nine X-ray observations of NGC 1142 over ~20 years, including five from a new NuSTAR+XMM-Newton monitoring campaign (2024-2025), using physically-motivated torus models UXCLUMPY, XSKIRTor, and RXTorusD to model the spectra and measure line-of-sight column density variability.
AI.result: The results confirm previously observed trends that the probability of observing NH variability increases with the number of observations and that variability magnitude depends on the timescale between observations. The observed trends are compared to simulated obscuration curves assuming different cloud locations and distributions.
AI.conclusion: The NH variability analysis of NGC 1142 supports existing variability trends and the comparison with simulated obscuration curves helps constrain the location and distribution of obscuring clouds around the AGN.

title: Characterizing the disruption of Böotes III: a missing link in the Galactic halo?
summary: The Böotes III (Boo3) dwarf galaxy has long been suspected of being the progenitor of Styx, a ~50°-long stellar stream that was simultaneously discovered in the same region of sky. Boo3's diffuse morphology, large velocity dispersion, small pericenter, and excess of candidate stars at large radii suggest it is undergoing active tidal disruption. A link to Styx is therefore logical; however, a clear connection between these structures has not yet been clearly demonstrated. Here, we re-examine the Boo3-Styx association by searching for Boo3's tidal debris using a combination of Gaia-selected members, new CaHK narrow-band imaging with CFHT/MegaCam, and stellar tracer catalogues of blue horizontal branch and red giant branch stars. We also conduct a broad search for a putative stream using matched filter techniques applied to SDSS DR17 and DELVE DR2. Despite our extensive search, we find no observational evidence directly linking Boo3 to Styx. Furthermore, our results suggest that either Boo3's extended substructure is too diffuse to be detected with current data, or that its particular orbit may have erased a coherent tidal signature. Boo3 thus remains an enigmatic system, and exemplifies the need for spectroscopic follow-up to properly disentangle the nature between this faint Milky Way satellite and nearby stream.

AI.tldr: This paper re-examines the suspected association between the Boötes III (Boo3) dwarf galaxy and the Styx stellar stream using Gaia-selected members, new CaHK narrow-band CFHT/MegaCam imaging, stellar tracer catalogues, and matched filter searches in SDSS DR17 and DELVE DR2. Despite extensive searches, no observational evidence directly linking Boo3 to Styx is found, suggesting either Boo3's extended substructure is too diffuse for current data or its orbit may have erased any coherent tidal signature. Boo3 remains enigmatic and requires spectroscopic follow-up to disentangle its nature from the nearby stream.
AI.motivation: Boo3 has long been suspected as the progenitor of the Styx stream due to its diffuse morphology, large velocity dispersion, small pericenter, and excess of candidate stars at large radii—all hallmarks of active tidal disruption. However, a clear connection between these structures has not yet been conclusively demonstrated, motivating this systematic re-examination.
AI.method: The study combines multiple datasets: Gaia-selected members, new CaHK narrow-band imaging from CFHT/MegaCam, and stellar tracer catalogues of blue horizontal branch (BHB) and red giant branch (RGB) stars. A broad search for a putative stream is also conducted using matched filter techniques applied to SDSS DR17 and DELVE DR2 data.
AI.result: Despite the extensive multi-dataset search, no observational evidence directly linking Boo3 to Styx is found. The results suggest either that Boo3's extended substructure is too diffuse to be detected with current data, or that its particular orbit may have erased any coherent tidal signature.
AI.conclusion: Boo3 remains an enigmatic system that exemplifies the need for spectroscopic follow-up to properly disentangle the nature of this faint Milky Way satellite and its relationship to the nearby Styx stream.
